newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Murdoch's rebel league agrees on peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Murdoch's rebel league agrees on peace plan.

text.p: Australia's two warring rugby league competitions, who are estimated to have spent over A$500 million (US$365 million) of their pay television backers' money fighting each other, on Thursday moved a step closer to a peace deal.
Rupert Murdoch's 10 Super League clubs have agreed to an amended Australian Rugby League (ARL) peace plan for a unified competition in 1998, said a Super League spokeswoman.
The spokeswoman said the 10 News Corp-funded clubs had agreed to support the peace plan offered on Wednesday night by the ARL, the sport's national governing body.
"Our clubs were briefed on the proposal during a telephone hook-up this morning and have agreed in principle to support it," Rebecca Wilson told Reuters.
"At this stage there is nothing more we can say about it, it's now up to the ARL clubs to consider it," she said.
The ARL, funded by pay television and telecommunications group Optus Communications, met Murdoch's Super League on Wednesday night and both issued statements on Thursday saying a deal was close.
Both the ARL and Super League said they agreed to refer the peace plan to their respective clubs after making amendments to an original ARL peace proposal at the Sydney meeting.
"The ARL and News Ltd today considered an ARL proposal for a united and fully integrated competition in 1998," the ARL said in a statement issued early on Thursday.
But details about the meeting were not made public.

However, Murdoch's Daily Telegraph newspaper in Sydney said on Thursday it understood the ARL had agreed to let Super League control the game's finances in return for the day-to-day running of the game.
ARL spokesman John Brady said the 12 ARL-loyal clubs would discuss the proposal later this week.
Brady told Reuters that the plan did not address the emotive issue of how many clubs would be needed in a unified competition or the question of television rights.
Super League wants to establish an elite 12-team competition but the ARL wants a minimum of 16 clubs and the consensus among media commentators is that they will reach a 14-team compromise.

News is believed to have committed about A$400 million to set up and run the rebel league in Australia and the established leagues in New Zealand, Britain and France with which Super League is aligned.

The established ARL, which fought News' attempt to set up Super League, is backed by Foxtel-competitor Optus Vision, which was recently fully merged with Optus Communications, Telstra's main competitor.
Optus is thought to have spent about A$120 million funding the 12 ARL clubs in the main competition and the ARL itself.
The main satellite pay television operator, Australis Media Ltd , has agreed to a merger with Foxtel.
